extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematically-interested readers evaluating or studying methods for circle quadrature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles to judge arguments, experiments, and approximations used in attempts to determine the relation between a circle's diameter and its circumference / area (quadrature of the circle). Emphasis on logical proof vs approximation, experimental design, and the validity of assumptions underlying polygonal approximation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of circle properties
rubrics_metrics.description: "The property of one circle is the property of all circles."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any claimed numerical relation between diameter and circumference (or area) must hold for every circle irrespective of scale; arguments should be tested at different magnitudes (the author uses radii of 1 mile, 100 miles, 10,000 miles to illustrate). The page uses scale arguments to expose contradictions in certain approximation-based methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish approximation from proof; require exact justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate equality of values obtained from inscribed and circumscribed polygons does not constitute a proof of a definable exact relation between diameter and circumference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly warns that obtaining closely matching numerical approximations (e.g., via polygons of many sides) is not a substitute for a rigorous demonstration that the circle's circumference-to-diameter ratio is a definable exact quantity. Do not infer exact equality from numerical convergence without proving the limiting relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on unproven assumptions (mean-proportional fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that the mean proportional between the areas of an inscribed and circumscribed polygon equals the area of a polygon with doubled number of sides is 'an assumption without the slightest proof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using the standard construction (alternate mean proportionals to double the number of sides) one must supply a proof that the algebraic/mean-proportional step corresponds to the geometric polygon with doubled sides. The page identifies this particular step as unjustified and central to the 'popular proof' fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isoperimetric / maximality principle as a criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The circumference of a circle cannot be rearranged into any other form so as to enclose an equal or larger area: the circle yields the largest area for a given perimeter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the elastic-line thought experiment: an elastic line arranged as a rectangle or any other shape cannot enclose an equal area to that enclosed when arranged as a circle. This serves as a conceptual check on claims that reshaping a circumference could yield the same area under different forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale-consistency test (check for physical absurdities at large scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that purport to show equality at small scales must remain sensible at very large scales; if a construction implies absurd large-scale geometry (e.g., polygon sides nearly miles long yet claiming equality within tiny fractional area), the method is suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses a radius of 10,000 miles to show that polygon-side linear sizes implied by the polygon-approximation argument would be macroscopic (≈1.9–2 miles) and asks how such polygons could both be inscribed in and circumscribed about the circle while having areas equal to the circle within tiny fractional errors. Test algorithms and arguments by scaling them up to reveal inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful treatment of numerical approximations and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic symbols and constants used as 'close approximations' (e.g., '7854') must not be treated as exact without acknowledging the approximation and its effect on conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When switching between the author's 'true theory' numbers (e.g., 78125 based figures) and 'orthodox' approximations (e.g., 7854/10000), explicitly record whether values are exact or approximations and propagate approximation error. Do not conflate approximate numeric coincidence with equality of geometric quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and control physical experiments rigorously
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple mechanical tests (measuring tape, stakes, wrapping wire) can be fallacious due to manufacturing imperfections; experimental proofs require careful control of material uniformity, precision machining, and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author proposes concrete experimental safeguards: cast an iron plate of uniform thickness, machine/plane surfaces, convert portions into a disc and rectangles, weigh to compare areas (mass proportional to surface area given uniform thickness/density). Also recommends wire-thread wrapping and repeated revolutions carefully recorded. Experiments must control density, thickness, and surface irregularities to be meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize manufactured objects approximate polygons of many sides
rubrics_metrics.description: A physically manufactured 'true' disc is, in practice, a polygon of a very large number of sides; wire wrapped about it will show 'angles' when unwrapped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting physical-measurement experiments, account for surface roughness and finite resolution: the 'disc' and the 'wire' will have microscopic irregularities that affect measured lengths. This cautions against assuming laboratory-measured equality implies ideal geometric equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concise illustrative examples; avoid overburdening
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and arrange illustrations so as to clearly elucidate the theory without becoming tedious; additional demonstrations are optional and should be used sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For exposition and pedagogy, choose a representative set of clear examples that make the point; excessive redundancy may distract without adding value. The author emphasizes clarity and brevity in presenting counterexamples and demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect privacy/consent when publishing correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish private letters or use a correspondent's name without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correspondent explicitly objects to having his name used in published letters. For published mathematical correspondence, obtain permission before making private exchanges public.
